stocks.note: Numbers as of market close May 4th.
stocks.news: Amazon (AMZN +1.41%) is opening up its shipping network to outside brands under a new "Amazon Supply Chain Service," covering freight, warehousing, and parcel delivery. P&G (PG -2.61%), 3M (MMM -0.66%), and American Eagle (AEO -3.19%) have already signed on. The reaction in the carrier names was brutal: UPS (UPS -10.47%) and FedEx (FDX -9.11%) both dropped double digits as investors reset expectations for what the parcel oligopoly looks like with Amazon as a third competitor instead of a customer. Separately, Palantir (PLTR +1.36%) beat both top and bottom lines after the bell, with revenue up 85% year-over-year, the biggest single-quarter jump since its 2020 debut. The bid is U.S. government contracts.

economy.note: US 10-Year and Gold as of 4:00 PM ET May 4th; WTI Crude reflects today's intraday move via investing.com.
economy.commentary:
Sugar is the new tell. Raw sugar futures hit a one-month high after Brazil's mills started diverting cane to ethanol production, a direct downstream effect of crude staying elevated through the Iran conflict. The 2026 surplus forecast just got cut from 3.4 million tonnes to 1.1 million. Snacks, sodas, and candy will reflect that within two quarters, which is one more line item working against household budgets going into the second half.

Crude itself eased today, WTI sitting near $102.56 (-3.63%) on softer demand prints, but the structural overhang is still the Strait of Hormuz. Kalshi traders just pushed the reopening bet from July to September. Treasury Secretary Bessent is publicly pressing China to help unblock it, since 90% of Iranian crude lands there. Trump and Xi meet May 14 in Beijing.

Wage data tells the same story from a different angle. New college grads expect a $80,000 starting salary; the actual average is $56,153, a $24,000 gap. Average starting pay rose 5.5% year-over-year to $68,873, with computer science leading at $81,535. The expectations gap matters for housing because first-time-buyer affordability math runs on actual paychecks, not the survey.

The 10-Year drifted up to 4.43% (+0.05%). Gold rolled back 2.41% to $4,532 as risk-on rotation took some shine off safe-haven positioning.

crypto.note: Numbers as of 4:00 PM ET on May 4th.
crypto.commentary:
Bitcoin punched back through $80,000 for the first time since January 31st, propelled by a legislative breakthrough rather than a flow story. Lawmakers reworked the CLARITY Act to thread a stablecoin needle: crypto firms cannot pay savings-style yield on idle stablecoins, but they can still pay rewards for trading, staking, and active usage. That compromise was enough to unstick the broader bill, which had been parked for months.

The market read it as bullish for the rails. Circle (CRCL +19.89%) ripped 20% intraday on the stablecoin clarity. Coinbase (COIN +6.14%) joined the move. ETH and XRP both rallied alongside Bitcoin on the policy tailwind, with XRP giving back some of its gain into the close.

real_estate.homebuilder: Bad Apple, Same Math: Why Affordability Is The Story Everywhere
real_estate.commentary:
Market Briefs led with NYC today, and the number is worth pausing on: it takes $145,000 a year to afford the median NYC rent, $60,000 more than the median household earns. New York lost 12,000 residents in 2025, the first drop since the pandemic. Less population means less tax revenue, which hits muni bonds, transit, and commercial real estate downstream. The same gravitational math is the spine of the Bay Area's flat-to-down stretches: when the affordability gap is structural, the answer is not a rate cut, it's price discovery.

The other story north of the border lines up: only 10% of Canadian retirees plan to downsize in the next decade. Selling costs eat ~15% of the proceeds (agent fees plus transfer taxes plus moving), and three of four older Canadians are using their savings to subsidize the next generation instead. California has the same friction with the same outcome: tenured owners stay put, supply stays tight, and the move-up rung breaks for the buyer one notch below.

Rates eased a hair today. The 30-year sits at 6.54%, the 15-year at 6.04%. Buyers actively shopping right now have already accepted the rate environment. They are qualified, committed, and they are not the rate-cut buyer.
